entries.clue: Church at rear of Newcastle United’s ground (6)

annotation.definitionFit: Chewed food has been ground between the teeth, and 'ground' is the past tense of grind, matching the tense of the answer.

indicatorNotes.at rear of: The rear of anything is its back end, so only the final letter of the word named next is taken.

blocks.note: ch is the short form printed on maps beside a church
the letter at the back of Newcastle
a couple united in marriage are wed

annotation.surface: The church standing behind the stadium where Newcastle United play.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Newcastle United' begs to be read as one thing, the football club whose ground the surface points at, and the setter splits the name in half. Only the last letter of the first half survives.

entries.clue: In truth, a Hampshire country estate feature (2-2)

annotation.definitionFit: A ha-ha is the sunken ditch-and-wall fence at the edge of an English country-house lawn, keeping livestock off the garden without a hedge to spoil the view.

indicatorNotes.In: 'In' says the letters are sitting inside the words that follow, unbroken and in the order given.

blocks.note: the four letters run on from the tail of the first word into the head of the last, across both the comma and the word break

annotation.surface: An assurance about something you would find on a Hampshire estate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In truth' reads as an aside promising honesty, which is exactly why the eye skims it. The name is said to come from the cry of surprise let out by anyone who nearly walks into one.

entries.clue: Disheartened Brummie enters spouting ‘Good health!’ (9)

annotation.definitionFit: Wellbeing is the state of being well — good health widened out to cover a person's whole condition, body and mind.

indicatorNotes.Disheartened: A disheartened word has had its heart torn out, leaving only what stood at either end.
indicatorNotes.enters: Whatever enters a place ends up inside it, so these letters land within the other chunk rather than beside it.

blocks.note: water welling up from the ground is water spouting, and the word opens after its fourth letter
Brummie stripped of everything between its first and last letter

annotation.surface: A man from Birmingham bursting in mid-flow with a toast.
annotation.walkthrough: Brummie is the setter's own pseudonym as well as a native of Birmingham, and here it is only a word to gut. 'Spouting' looks like the talking the Brummie is doing and means a spring of water.

entries.clue: Force gets you finally in gear (6)

annotation.definitionFit: Duress is force applied to make somebody act — a confession under duress is one squeezed out by threat.

indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at the end of the word just given, so only its last letter is taken.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts the letter just found inside the word that follows rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: gear is clothing, and the word opens after its first letter
the last letter of you

annotation.surface: Pressure that finally gets somebody into their kit.
annotation.walkthrough: On the surface 'in gear' is the idiom about getting moving, and the wordplay needs gear in its older sense of clothing. 'You' is not the solver being addressed, just a word with a last letter.

entries.clue: City fans unruly but free from sin? (8)

annotation.definitionFit: To sanctify is to make holy, and making someone holy is precisely freeing them from sin.

indicatorNotes.unruly: An unruly crowd will not keep its lines, and letters described that way will not keep their order either.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Supporters of a football club behaving badly at the ground.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital C sends you hunting for a particular club when the word is only there to be stirred. The question mark admits the definition is a whole phrase rather than a single word.

entries.clue: Classic film debut of Sesame Street not established internally (6,9)

annotation.definitionFit: Sunset Boulevard is Billy Wilder's 1950 picture about a forgotten silent star, long since fixed in the canon of classics.

indicatorNotes.debut of: A debut is a first appearance, so what is wanted is the letter the word makes its entrance with.
indicatorNotes.internally: Internally means in the middle rather than at either end, so this chunk drops in between the two pieces around it.

blocks.note: the opening letter of Sesame, taken on its own
something not yet set — jelly, concrete, a date in the diary — is unset
a boulevard is a broad street lined with trees

annotation.surface: A famous film making its first appearance on Sesame Street, where nothing has been settled indoors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sesame Street' is one title in the reader's head, so splitting it is the whole difficulty: only Sesame is used, and the other half is the word for street. Norma Desmond's line about being big while the pictures got small comes from this film.

entries.clue: Meant to change some lines for worm (8)

annotation.definitionFit: A nematode is a roundworm, so 'worm' is the everyday name for the creature the answer gives the scientific one for.

indicatorNotes.to change: A thing told to change does not come back as it went in, and letters change by swapping places.

blocks.note: the five letters rearranged
an ode is a poem, which is some lines of verse

annotation.surface: An actor who intended to rewrite a few of his lines.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Meant to change' reads as an intention never carried out, which is how the instruction hides in plain sight. ODE is the crossword's standard answer whenever lines are wanted.

entries.clue: Tight garment cut in circles (5)

annotation.definitionFit: A tunic is the close-fitting jacket of a soldier's or police officer's uniform, so 'tight' describes the cut and 'garment' the thing itself.

indicatorNotes.circles: Something that circles keeps going round, and letters sent round like that come back in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters

annotation.surface: A clinging garment cut on the round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like tailoring and is fodder instead, which leaves the entire wordplay in two short words the eye runs straight past. Five letters from five letters, with nothing else in the clue.

entries.clue: It can douse the flames of passion – e.g. with nine shakes (4,6)

annotation.definitionFit: A fire engine is the truck that turns out to put a blaze out, so the definition names it by the job it exists to do.

indicatorNotes.shakes: A thing that shakes has its parts thrown out of place, and letters shaken settle in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: fire is passion itself — a speech delivered with fire
anagram fodder: the abbreviation without its stops, plus the number written out

annotation.surface: Whatever it is that kills a romance, nine good shakes of it will do the job.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash lets the second half pass as an example of the first when it is a set of instructions. 'Flames of passion' is one phrase on the surface and is torn in two by the parsing.

entries.clue: South American country seizes medic and, briefly, kids (8)

annotation.definitionFit: Kids is the informal word every parent uses for their children, and both are plural nouns for the young of the family.

indicatorNotes.seizes: To seize something is to grab hold of it, and what is grabbed ends up held inside.
indicatorNotes.briefly: Said briefly, a word shrinks to the shortest form people actually pronounce.

blocks.note: Chile is the long strip down the Pacific coast, and it opens after its fourth letter
dr is the doctor's title in front of a name
and spoken in a hurry is 'n', as in rock 'n' roll

annotation.surface: A Latin American state arresting a doctor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kids' at the end looks like a verb — the country is joking — and it is the plural noun being defined. The commas around 'briefly' let a piece of wordplay pass as an aside.

entries.clue: Crew on capsized craft chant (6)

annotation.definitionFit: A mantra is a formula chanted over and over in meditation, so 'chant' names it by the only thing it is ever used for.

indicatorNotes.capsized: A capsized boat has turned right over, so the word it applies to is written backwards.

blocks.note: to man a boat is to crew it
craft is art, turned round

annotation.surface: The crew clinging to an upturned boat and chanting.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is nautical, which is what makes 'craft' look like the boat when it means skill. Crossword setters use craft for art so often it is worth filing away.

entries.clue: Like the Two Ronnies’ big show in base (12)

annotation.definitionFit: Both Ronnies wore heavy dark spectacles on screen, so being like them is being bespectacled — a definition by example rather than a synonym.

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' drops what has just been clued inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: the bed of a machine or a road is the base it rests on, and it splits after its second letter
a spectacle is a show staged on a grand scale

annotation.surface: The Two Ronnies putting on a lavish revue at a military base.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Base' invites the army camp the surface wants and means the foundation something rests on. Ronnie Barker and Ronnie Corbett fronted BBC sketch comedy for two decades.

entries.clue: Nebulous picture of cold, obtrusive, southern promontory (10)

annotation.definitionFit: A cloudscape is a picture whose subject is the sky, and nebulous is the adjective for cloud, so the definition says cloud-picture twice over.

blocks.note: c is the cold tap and the cold wash
a loud tie is an obtrusive one
s is the compass point on any map
a cape is the headland that juts into the sea

annotation.surface: A hazy painting of a bleak, overbearing headland down south.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas make a list of adjectives, which is why four separate instructions read as one description of a coast. 'Nebulous' belongs to the definition and does the misleading anyway, meaning vague on the surface and cloudy in the answer.

entries.clue: Southern French town omits one from legal defence (4)

annotation.definitionFit: Albi is the cathedral city on the Tarn in south-west France, so the definition places the answer by country and region.

indicatorNotes.omits: To omit something is to leave it out, so the letter named next never reaches the answer.

blocks.note: an alibi is the defence that you were somewhere else, and this is the word before anything goes
one in Roman numerals is I, and that is the letter left out

annotation.surface: A town in the south of France leaving something out of its legal case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Southern French' looks like the language of the Midi and turns out to be plain geography. Albi gave its name to the Albigensian heretics crushed there in the thirteenth century.

entries.clue: Wicked, popular, mature repartee (8)

annotation.definitionFit: Badinage is light teasing talk, which is repartee in its everyday sense — quick exchanges made for amusement rather than for winning.

blocks.note: wicked and bad are the same charge
what is in this season is what is popular
to mature is to age, as cheese and whisky do

annotation.surface: Three verdicts in a row on somebody's banter.
annotation.walkthrough: The adjectives run on so smoothly that the sentence reads as praise for a person's talk rather than as three separate words to write down. 'Mature' is the verb to age, not the adjective.

entries.clue: Teddy possibly exploding with anger (9)

annotation.definitionNote: A teddy is one garment where nightwear is the uncountable class it belongs to, and 'possibly' is the setter's flag that the definition offers an example.
annotation.definitionFit: A teddy is a one-piece camisole and knickers worn in bed, which makes it one item of nightwear.

indicatorNotes.exploding: Something exploding throws its parts everywhere, and the letters come down in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: A teddy bear blowing up in a rage.
annotation.walkthrough: The teddy is a bear on the surface and a woman's one-piece in the answer, which is what 'possibly' is there to license. 'With' belongs to the fodder rather than joining the halves.

entries.clue: Thousands of pounds prior to working – it’s all relative (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a person and the definition is a catchphrase; 'relative' is the word doing the work, dressed up as the saying about everything depending on how you look at it.
annotation.definitionFit: A grandson is a relative, and the idiom is bent so its last word means a member of the family rather than a matter of comparison.

indicatorNotes.prior to: Prior to means before, so the letters just clued are written in front of the ones that follow.

blocks.note: a grand is a thousand pounds in British slang, and several of them are grands
a machine that is working is on

annotation.surface: Serious money demanded up front, and a shrug about how serious it really is.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash lets the definition pass as a wry comment on the sum of money, which is the hardest place in a clue to spot one. 'Working' is the switched-on machine rather than the labour.

entries.clue: Peak month for initially tucking into ragu perhaps (8)

annotation.definitionFit: The Jungfrau is a mountain in the Bernese Alps above Interlaken, so 'peak' names the answer by its bare category.

indicatorNotes.initially: Initially asks for the letter a word starts with and nothing more of it.
indicatorNotes.tucking into: To tuck into something is to get right inside it, so the letter goes within the other word rather than beside it.
indicatorNotes.perhaps: Perhaps offers the word as a possibility rather than a fixed thing, which licenses any arrangement of its letters.

blocks.note: jun is June as the calendar prints it
the four letters of the sauce rearranged, then opened after the first
the letter for begins with

annotation.surface: The best month of the year for getting stuck into a plate of ragu.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is an unusual anagram indicator, and it catches solvers because in most clues it flags a definition by example instead. 'Peak month' reads as one phrase and only the first word of it defines.

entries.clue: Working to dispose of international medal (4)

annotation.definitionFit: Gong is British slang for a medal or decoration — the word used for an honour collected at the palace.

indicatorNotes.to dispose of: To dispose of something is to get rid of it, so the letter named next is thrown out of the word.

blocks.note: a machine that is working is going, and this is the word before the loss
international is I, the letter disposed of

annotation.surface: A campaign to do away with some international award.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Working to dispose of' reads as the effort being spent on the abolition, and 'working' is only the state of a machine that has been switched on. I for international comes from football caps and cricket sides.

entries.clue: Fairy king goes in through part of tower (6)

annotation.definitionFit: The belfry is the stage of a tower where the bells hang, so it is one part of the structure rather than the whole of it.

indicatorNotes.goes in: What goes in is placed inside, so the letters just clued sit within the word that follows.

blocks.note: to travel by a place is to travel through it, and the two letters open up to take the rest

r is rex, Latin for king, the letter monarchs sign after their name

annotation.surface: A fairy king making his way in through the tower.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fairy king' reads as one person, Oberon in the wood, and splits into two separate pieces. 'Through' is the preposition the picture needs and a two-letter word in the wordplay.

entries.clue: Fancy teen’s garment split (12)

annotation.definitionFit: An estrangement is a split between people who were once close — a split in a family, a couple's split — the noun for the breach itself.

indicatorNotes.Fancy: Fancy work is elaborate rather than plain, and letters given the fancy treatment do not stay in their plain order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters once the apostrophe is dropped

annotation.surface: An ornate outfit for a teenager, slit down one side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Split' comes last and reads as one more detail of the garment, which is where the definition hides. The apostrophe counts for nothing when the letters are gathered up.

entries.clue: Become entangled with party on left (5)

annotation.definitionFit: To ravel is to become tangled or knotted, the state loose thread works itself into when nobody is watching.

indicatorNotes.on: In a down clue, whatever sits on something else is written above it, so these letters go on top.

annotation.surface: Getting tangled up with a party of the left.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party on left' reads as politics and the party is the all-night kind. Ravel faces both ways as a word — it can mean to tangle and to untangle — and the clue takes the tangling sense.

entries.clue: Second vehicle provides wound protection (4)

blocks.note: s is the second on a stopwatch

annotation.surface: A back-up car that turns up carrying the first-aid kit.

entries.clue: Doorstep lacking its end material (6)

entries.clue: A large French supermarket has no opening outside (8)

entries.clue: Ruled again to recruit Conservative, being laid back (8)

annotation.definitionFit: To recline is to lean back until you are lying down, so somebody reclined has literally been laid back against the seat.

entries.clue: Rocky Bay houses our poor African people (6)

annotation.surface: A rocky bay giving shelter to the poor of Africa.
